analysis.title: "No Obvious Solve": Goldman Says AI's Cost Of Capital Has "Objectively Repriced" As Hyperscalers Face Their Financing Week
key_insights: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky (EMEA head of delta-one trading) says AI demand remains strong but the cost of capital has "objectively repriced" with no obvious solution. Hyperscaler and data center credit spreads have widened across the capital structure.

Alphabet and Microsoft report Wednesday and Amazon Thursday. Privorotsky says the focus is on how backlog converts to cloud revenue and how the next leg of capex gets financed, not only whether capex intentions hold.

Privorotsky's four scenarios for hyperscaler capex: (1) worst, capex accelerates funded by expensive debt, (2) arguably worse, capex is cut because financing is unavailable, (3) middle, capex flat or up with more equity financing (bad for hyperscaler equity, potentially good for credit), (4) best, capex rises alongside accelerating organic cash flow with a path to self-funding through 2027/28.

The article argues a capex cut forced by a closed financing window is not bullish for anyone, because the buildout the market is priced for could not be funded. Zero Hedge's view is that the likely outcome this week is a mix of the worst case and the middle ground, with capex guides rising and the gap filled with pricier debt, off-balance-sheet vehicles and equity.

Bloomberg reported Meta is seeking up to $95B in equity to fund AI spending. Consensus models roughly $140B of Meta capex, above operating cash flow, and Meta's 5-year CDS has roughly doubled since August to about 120bps and hit a record last week.
Goldman's 30-year Hyperscaler basket hit new wides and trades +85bps cheap to the IG100 ex-Hyperscaler basket, a 90bps move since the basket launched in February.
Goldman's custom baskets desk said on Oct 17 that AI credit was pricing a 15% drop in hyperscaler equities, and that spreads have since gone wider.

AI-related USD high yield spreads have decoupled from the rest of junk. Average CCC yields topped 16% on Friday for the first time since 2020, and last week's 1.6% junk loss was the biggest in 18 months (Bloomberg).

Elon Musk said debt markets have "almost entirely shut off access to money" for companies without substantial non-AI-data-center revenue and that the 200+ neoclouds face consolidation. Pricing on SpaceX's $40B GPU debt deal was reportedly still being negotiated (Bloomberg). CoreWeave was down another 5% premarket per Goldman's TMT desk.

Positioning: US equities sold for a third consecutive week, the largest single-stock de-grossing since July. TMT sold about $20B over two weeks, approaching the $23B sold in July's AI selling episode. Fundamental nets are at YTD lows but gross is at the 63rd percentile. Global tech selling was -3.3σ over two weeks with long sales outpacing short covers 3.4:1.

Goldman's Risk Appetite Indicator saw one of its largest drops on record and is at its lowest since April of last year. The NDX-SPX implied vol spread is near 5-year highs (98th percentile). There was little rotation into defensives.
Last week the Russell rose 2%, equal-weight S&P gained 1.1%, Nasdaq fell 70bps and SOX fell 3.2%. Privorotsky: "shorts squeezing, nothing working."

Catalysts: hyperscaler guidance and the Fed, with risks two-sided on both. WIRP puts the odds of an FOMC hike Wednesday at 11% and the 10-year is just under 5%. The question is whether Warsh focuses on recent hot inflation or on tightening financial conditions.

Street views differ. Goldman's custom baskets desk calls this a HF deleveraging episode and recommends buying the dip in Power, Hyperscalers, Inference and Cyber. Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson sees AI concerns as one of three clearing events that could end the correction. HSBC's Max Kettner cut equities to tactically neutral, citing hyperscaler free cash flow as a swing factor into 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's custom baskets desk says the market is in a HF deleveraging episode where short-term stops matter more than medium-term value, and recommends buying the dip in Power, Hyperscalers, Inference and Cyber. Privorotsky stays optimistic on demand, and the best case is capex rising with accelerating organic cash flow and a path to self-funding through 2027/28.
tension_points.bear_case: The cost of capital has objectively repriced with no obvious solve. Hyperscaler spreads are at new wides, Meta's capex runs ahead of operating cash flow, and a forced capex cut would mean the buildout cannot be funded.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscaler guidance this week (Alphabet and Microsoft Wednesday, Amazon Thursday) showing capex rising alongside accelerating organic cash flow would support the bull case. A capex cut forced by unavailable financing would be worse for the bull case.
